Persis
PUR-sis
proper noun
From the Greek Persis, “a Persian woman,” a name marking origin or descent.

📖 Biblical Definition

Persis is greeted by Paul as “the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.” Two things lift her commendation above the others in this passage. First, she is called “the beloved” — though notably Paul writes “the beloved,” not “my beloved” as with the men, a fitting modesty in greeting a woman. Second, where Tryphena and Tryphosa “labour” in the present, Persis “laboured much” in the past tense and with the added measure of “much” — a long, abundant, completed record of toil for the gospel. Her name means “a Persian woman,” suggesting she or her forebears came from the East, perhaps once a slave brought to Rome, now a beloved and tireless servant of Christ. The Reformed reader honors in Persis the faithful woman of long service, the saint whose labor is not a season but a lifetime, who “laboured much” without grasping office or seeking notice. The added word “much” is the Spirit’s own commendation of abundant, persevering work. Persis appears only here, yet her single verse crowns a life of toil. Her name teaches the church to prize the long-faithful over the briefly brilliant, and to remember that God measures not the splendor of our work but its faithfulness and abundance. To have laboured much in the Lord, beloved by the saints, is a record that outshines every earthly distinction and stands written in heaven.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A believing woman at Rome whom Paul greets as “the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.”

expand to see more

PERSIS, a Christian woman at Rome saluted by Paul as “the beloved.”

Commended as one “which laboured much in the Lord” (Rom 16:12).

Her name means “a Persian woman,” marking eastern origin or descent.

Paul writes “the beloved,” not “my beloved,” a fitting modesty.

The added “much” commends abundant, long-continued toil (Rom 16:12).

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:12 — "Salute Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord."

1Co 15:58 — "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Gal 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Rev 14:13 — "And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is the high worth of the long-faithful woman who laboured much in the Lord across a lifetime.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Persis is the worth of long, abundant labor in the Lord. The Spirit’s own word “much” commends not a season of zeal but a lifetime of toil. Persis, perhaps once a slave brought from the East, became a beloved and tireless servant of Christ, and Scripture honors her for it.

The church is tempted to prize the briefly brilliant over the long-faithful, but God measures work by its faithfulness and abundance, not its splendor. Persis grasped no office and sought no notice; she simply laboured much in the Lord. Her works follow her, for the dead who die in the Lord rest from their labours, and that record stands written in heaven forever.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name Persis simply means “a Persian woman,” a name of national origin.

expand to see more

Persis — Greek for “a Persian woman,” marking eastern descent.

Such origin-names were often given to slaves brought from foreign lands.

“Laboured” renders the Greek kopiao, to toil to weariness, here in past tense.

The qualifier “much” (polla) marks abundant, surpassing toil.

The shift to past tense crowns a completed life of faithful service.

Usage

"Persis laboured much in the Lord, a lifetime of toil crowned in a single verse."

"Paul honored Persis not for a season’s zeal but for abundant, long-continued labor."

"The aged saint was a Persis, beloved and tireless, her works following her to glory."
